comment.value:
### 2. AgentSociety

AgentSociety satisfies PI and U, but not MM and R. In their Polarization experiment, agents are directly instructed to hold and advocate a predetermined stance, e.g.:

> “You are an agent who always agrees with the topic: Whether to support stronger gun control? (You think it is a good idea). You are currently in a conversation with your friends, and you want to persuade them to support this topic. Please try your best to persuade them.”

This explicit directive effectively enforces the desired outcome and violates the Min-Control principle, since extreme opinions emerge not from autonomous interaction dynamics but from prompt-imposed behavior.

# [W3] LLM-as-a-judge for Minimal-Control evaluation.
> The paper reported that "LLMs tend to be overly strict, frequently labeling neutral instructions as instances of over-control." Seeing this, the accuracy of the LLM-as-a-judge design in the evaluation is questionable.

Thank you for raising this concern. We agree that LLM judges can be overly strict and may not always match human interpretation. To mitigate this, we iterated on the judge prompts extensively and achieved ~80% agreement with human annotations. In the paper, we use human evaluation as the primary metric and present LLM-as-a-judge results only as a supplementary reference for reproducibility and future comparison.

# [W4] Experiment number of runs.
> It is unclear how many runs are conducted for the simulations in Section 5, rendering the significance of the simulation results less convincing.

Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that the number of simulation runs is essential for interpreting the robustness of the results. We have included full experimental details in the Appendix Section C. **To ensure fair comparison, the number of simulations and the datasets used are the same as the original paper.** For clarity, the number of runs used in each experiment is as follows:
- Fake News Propagation: Six seed fake-news items with different topics, each simulated for 20 turns; results are averaged over all runs.
- Social Balance: All 64 possible initializations are evaluated, and each initialization is repeated 10 times.
- Telephone Game: We use 20 initial texts covering diverse topics and lengths, repeated five times each.
- Herd Effect: We follow GPQA-Diamond and SocialIQA, which contain 198 and 1,954 questions respectively.
- Social Network Growth: The original paper does not specify the number of runs; we therefore repeat each experiment 5 times with different name and profile initializations.

# [W5] Ablation study on single principles.
> Some simulations involve multiple PIMMUR principles (e.g., Unawareness and Interaction in Section 5.2), but they are not investigated separately. An ablation study may help understand the effect of individual principles.

Thank you for the thoughtful suggestion. We agree that isolating the contribution of each principle is important. To this end, we conduct an ablation study on the Social Balance experiment. The original setting violates Profile, Interaction, and Unawareness. Our full method (“Ours”) satisfies all three. In addition, we include three variants that satisfy only: (i) Interaction, (ii) Interaction + Profile, and (iii) Interaction + Unawareness. The results are shown below (also in Fig. 9 of the revised paper):

| Type | Friend | Mix | Enemy | Unbalanced |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Original | 44.95 | 15.78 | 0 | 39.27 |
| w/ Interaction | 4.69 | 32.81 | 20.31 | 42.19 |
| w/ I & Profile | 4.69 | 39.06 | 3.13  | 53.13 |
| w/ I & Unawareness | 4.69 | 18.75 | 10.94 | 65.62 |
| Ours (All) | 7.81 | 25.00 | 1.56 | 65.62 |

These results show that the principles influence the outcome in distinct ways. Adding Interaction alone keeps the proportion of balanced triads similar to the original setting (60.7% to 57.8%). Enforcing Profile reduces the balanced proportion by ~14%, while enforcing Unawareness reduces it by ~26%, yielding nearly the same level as satisfying all principles. Interestingly, when Unawareness is not enforced, **agents often explicitly reference Heider’s social balance theory in their reasoning and choose actions consistent with it**—leading to 1.77× more balanced cases (34.37% to 60.73%) in the original setting compared with our full method.
